newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish Feb yr/yr inflation seen below 2.0 percent.
newsitem.headline: Irish Feb yr/yr inflation seen below 2.0 percent.

text.p: Ireland's consumer price index (CPI) is expected to show a rise of up to one percent in February after January's 0.5 percent fall, economists said on Wednesday.
But the year-on-year rate should come in comortably below two percent and ease fears of any immediate surge that might tarnish Ireland's EMU credentials, they said.

The Central Statistics Office (CSO) data, due at 1200 GMT on Thursday, is only the second time that monthly figures have been published and followed January's fall which caught many economists by surprise.
Some attributed January's unexpected dip of 0.5 percent to the effect of price cutting in January sales but have revised their opinons and marked year-on-year inflation downwards.
"Even allowing for the distortion of the sales, it was a genuine indication that inflation has not resurfaced as people had feared," said Eoin Fahy, economist with Ulster Bank Markets.
Fahy is forecasting a year on year rate of "just below two percent - 1.9 or even 1.8 percent".
Dan McLaughlin of stockbrokers Riada said that even allowing for the effect of the sales, the message from the January data was benign.
"People are revising their forecats downwards. Although it was difficult to interpret January's data because it was influenced by the sales, there was very little service inflation," he said.

Alan MacQuaid of Bloxham's stockbrokers is predicting a monthly rise of 0.5 percent for a year-on-year rate of 1.5 percent. "I'm of the view that inflation will be lower that most people believe," he said.

Economists said one concern on the inflation horizon was surging house prices which recorded an 18 percent increase in the third quarter of 1996 and are said by some estate agents to be forging ahead in the early part of this year. "We know house prices are very well bid and growth could be very strong. The real issue is whether or not they are going to spill over into the CPI data," McLaughlin said. The CSO data comes in the wake of Ireland's Central Bank's spring bulletin last week which said that although most current indicators of inflation were relatively stable, continuing viligance must be maintain against stimulating inflationary pressures.
It estimated, in its quarterly bulletin, that an expansionary January budget, offset by an appreciating nominal exchange rate, would translate into an average inflation rate of 2.3 percent for 1997.
